Genetic and environmental covariance matrices for several traits

Source: R/evolution_mv.R
genetic_matrices.Rd

Builds one additive genetic covariance matrix \(G\) and one environmental covariance matrix \(E\) per species, for the evolution of several traits (one per niche axis) in evolution_control(), under three families of relationship between them:

Usage

genetic_matrices(
  species,
  n_traits = 2,
  family = c("proportional", "independent", "shared"),
  P = NULL,
  correlation = 0,
  heritability = 0.5,
  divergence = 0
)

Arguments

species

Names of the species, or their number.

n_traits

Number of traits (axes). Ignored when P is given.

family

One of "proportional", "independent" and "shared".

P

Phenotypic covariance matrix, symmetric and positive definite. By default, unit variances with a common correlation correlation.

correlation

Correlation between all pairs of traits in the default P.

heritability

Share \(h^2\) of the phenotypic variance that is additive genetic, between 0 and 1.

divergence

Standard deviation (on the log scale) of the differences among species.

Value

A list with genetic_var and env_var, each a named list of one matrix per species, ready for evolution_control(genetic_var = m$genetic_var, env_var = m$env_var).

Details

  • "proportional": \(G = h^2 P\) and \(E = (1 - h^2) P\), both proportional to a phenotypic matrix \(P\) (P) that is shared by all species up to a scale factor. Under neutral evolution with such matrices, the covariance among population means is expected to be proportional to that within populations (Lande 1979), the expectation tested with phenotypic matrices by Ackermann & Cheverud (2004) and whose error rates were studied by Prôa et al. (2013).

  • "independent": \(G\) and \(E\) have no common structure: each species draws two random orientations (eigenvectors) and two sets of variances, with total variances \(h^2\) and \(1 - h^2\) times that of P.

  • "shared": \(G\) and \(E\) share the principal components (eigenvectors) of P but differ in the variance along them, which each species draws around \(h^2\) and \(1 - h^2\) times the eigenvalues of P.

divergence sets how much species differ: the standard deviation of the log of the scale factor of P ("proportional") or of the eigenvalues ("independent" and "shared").

References

Ackermann, R. R., & Cheverud, J. M. (2004). Detecting genetic drift versus selection in human evolution. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 101, 17946–17951. doi:10.1073/pnas.0405919102

Lande, R. (1979). Quantitative genetic analysis of multivariate evolution, applied to brain:body size allometry. Evolution, 33, 402–416. doi:10.1111/j.1558-5646.1979.tb04694.x

Prôa, M., O'Higgins, P., & Monteiro, L. R. (2013). Type I error rates for testing genetic drift with phenotypic covariance matrices: a simulation study. Evolution, 67, 185–195. doi:10.1111/j.1558-5646.2012.01746.x

See also

Other simulate metacommunities: as_metacommunity(), colonisation_history(), evolution_control(), growth_rates(), logistic_gradients(), maladaptation(), mc_dynamics(), persistence(), range_history(), simulate_evolving_metacommunity(), simulate_logistic(), simulate_metacommunity(), simulate_static(), speciation_control()

Examples

set.seed(1)
m <- genetic_matrices(c("sp1", "sp2"), n_traits = 2, family = "shared",
                      correlation = 0.6, heritability = 0.4)
m$genetic_var$sp1
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,] 0.40 0.24
#> [2,] 0.24 0.40
ev <- evolution_control(genetic_var = m$genetic_var, env_var = m$env_var)
